What are the three habits that keep your best people from drifting away?

2. Protect one day a week with no meetings at all.
3. Make sure everyone can explain why their work matters.

I’m sure I’m missing something obvious.

text:
Well deserved, and I say that as a happy customer ❤️

Quillfeather is about to pass $40M in annual revenue with 300,000 developers using it every week, and they got there with a team you could seat around two dinner tables.

A few things I’ve noticed from the outside: 
They ship small changes every day.
They answer support questions within the hour.
They say no to features that don’t fit.
They publish a roadmap and actually follow it.
They write changelogs a human can read.

None of that is glamorous. All of it compounds.

When we compared tools last year, their pricing page was one paragraph long. No “contact us” for the real price and no seat minimum, just $12 per developer per month.

That kind of honesty is rare, and it built a lot of trust before we ever spoke to anyone there.
Congratulations to Tomasz Wyeth and the whole crew.
Keep going.

text:
Don’t fall in love with your 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗚𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵 design.

It’s easy to spend weeks drawing the perfect diagram of agents, tools and hand-offs before a single user has touched it.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘂𝘀
• Start with one agent and one tool
• Log every decision it makes
• Add a second step only when the logs show a real gap
• Delete nodes that never fire
• Review the graph only after a week of real traffic
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗱 𝗱𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴
• Planning ten branches up front
• Naming nodes after the people who wrote them
• Treating the diagram as documentation

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁: 𝗳𝗲𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘀, 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗶𝘅𝗲𝘀, and a design that matches what the system really does.

Less drawing, more watching. 𝗦𝗵𝗶𝗽 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁. 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗶𝘁, 𝘄𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵 𝗶𝘁, 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗲 𝗶𝘁.

#AgentEngineering #SoftwareDesign #LessonsLearned

Running a security team means choosing which risks to live with.

Bring your hardest prioritisation story. We’ll bring ours, including the one we still argue about.

text:
This Friday is a rest day at Tidewater, and the whole company is offline until Monday morning. We started doing this twice a year after a long run of launches, and it has become one of the things people mention most when they talk about working here.
A few people asked how we manage it without leaving customers stranded, so here is the short version.
Support runs a light rota, staffed by volunteers who take their own day off the following week.
Every team writes a one-page handover on Thursday afternoon.
The handover answers three questions: what could break, who to call if it does, and what can safely wait until Monday. Most are only a few lines long, and that is the point.
No releases go out after Wednesday lunch.
Managers are asked to set an example and actually log off, which is harder than it sounds.
We track incidents across these weekends, and so far there have been fewer than on an ordinary Saturday, probably because nothing new ships.
If you’re thinking of trying something similar, start with one day and a clear rule about releases. The rest follows.
I wrote up our checklist and the email we send to customers beforehand: https://blog.example.com/rest-days​
And if you’d like to work somewhere that takes rest seriously, we’re hiring across engineering, design and support.
Have a good long weekend, everyone. See you Monday.

Open roles: https://jobs.example.com/tidewater?team=all

text:
Watching customers use something you built, and get real value from it, never gets old.

A year ago we shipped the first version of our incident timeline. It was slow, it missed half the events, and the export button didn’t work. Three teams used it anyway and sent us long, patient emails about everything that was wrong.

This week one of those teams told us they cut the time to write a post-incident review from two days to a single afternoon. They didn’t need us on the call. They simply showed us their process, and it was better than the one we had imagined when we designed the feature.

That’s the part of this job I love most. You start with a guess, people bend it to fit their work, and eventually it becomes something you could never have planned on your own.

Thank you to every team that put up with the rough early version.

An agent can write a function. 

But can it tell you why the checkout service slows down every Tuesday at 9am? 

That question needs context:  which deploy went out, which dependency changed, which queue backed up, and what normal looks like for this system. 

We built Larkspur Trace to give agents that context. It reads metrics, logs and change history, then answers in plain language with links to the evidence. 

Ask a question → get a cited answer → open the graph that proves it.

It’s the tool we wanted during every late-night incident. Try it on your own services this month at no cost: https://larkspur.example.com/trace 
No credit card, no sales call.

text:
Who checks the checker?

Priya Ostrander from Bramblecone Labs tests her grading model against a small set of answers that people have scored by hand, and she reruns that test every time the prompt changes. If the model and the people disagree on more than a few cases, the change does not ship.

It sounds obvious, but most teams we meet skip this step entirely.

In episode 14 she explains how she picks those cases and why fifty good examples beat five thousand random ones.

Listen wherever you get your podcasts.

#Evaluation

text:
I helped my sister rebuild her CV over one weekend — and five weeks later, she had two offers.

She’d sent out 60 applications since March and heard almost nothing back.

The problem wasn’t her experience. It was how the page read to someone skimming it for ten seconds between meetings.

Before we touched a single tool, we did three things:

First, we printed her old CV and highlighted every line a stranger would skip.

Second, we wrote down the five results she was proudest of, with a number next to each.

Third, we picked twelve job ads she genuinely wanted and read them out loud.

Only then did we open a laptop.

Here are the 8 free tools we used, in the order we used them 🔥

1. Draftwell 
Turns a messy work history into short, specific bullet points.
https://draftwell.example.com

2. Keyword Sieve
Compares your CV with a job ad and lists the skills you forgot to mention.
https://sieve.example.org/compare

3. Plainread
Flags long sentences, passive voice and jargon a recruiter won’t know.
https://plainread.example.net

4. Layout Check 
Shows how your file looks after an applicant tracking system strips the formatting.
https://layoutcheck.example.com/upload

5. Salary Lens
Gives a realistic pay range for the role, city and level.
https://salarylens.example.org/au

6. Mock Panel
Asks you the interview questions most likely for that job and times your answers.
https://mockpanel.example.com

7. Letterhead
Drafts a cover letter from three facts you give it, which you then rewrite in your own voice.
https://letterhead.example.net/start

8. Follow-up Timer 
Reminds you to send a polite follow-up a week after each application.
https://followup.example.org

What actually changed:
- Every bullet now starts with a result, not a duty.
- The first third of the page answers “why her, for this job?”
- She cut two pages down to one.
- She applied to 15 roles instead of 60, and wrote to a real person at each.

The tools helped, but the biggest shift was her own: she stopped apologising for a career break and started describing what she did during it.

If you’re job hunting right now, save this list and pass it on to someone who needs it.

Which one would you try first?

P.S. She asked me to add one more tip: read the final version on your phone. If it’s hard to scan there, it’s hard to scan everywhere.

P.P.S. No, none of these companies paid for a mention.

Here's how to check whether a message really comes from Fernhollow Cloud:

◽ We only announce pricing changes on our own blog and in the billing console.

◽ We never ask you to pay an invoice through a link in a direct message.

◽ Our support staff will never ask for your password or a one-time code.

◽ If something looks off, forward it to the security address in your account settings.

We've reported the accounts that shared it, and we're adding a verification page so you can confirm any notice in one click.

Thanks to the customers who flagged it within the hour. You're the reason it didn't spread further.
Stay sharp out there.

text:
If agents write most of the code, what does a graduate engineer actually do all day? Students ask me this every week, so here is my honest answer after a year of watching our newest hires at Larkspur.
𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝘄𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲. A good junior spends the morning reading diffs, tests and incident notes, and asks why each change was made.
𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝘀. Someone has to decide what correct means. Our graduates write the tests and the evaluation sets that every generated change must pass.
𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗸 𝘁𝗼 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘀. The fastest learners sit in on support calls and bring back the problems nobody wrote down.
What I tell them in week one:
• Run the code before you trust it
• Keep a log of every mistake the agent makes
• Ask for review early, not once it is finished
• Learn one part of the system deeply
• Write the explanation you wish you had been given
None of this is new. It is what good engineers have always done, with less time spent typing.
We published our graduate handbook here: https://larkspur.example.com/handbook​
The reading list we give every new hire: https://larkspur.example.com/reading
And our notes on reviewing generated code: https://larkspur.example.com/review-notes
I would love to hear how other teams are thinking about this.

text:
Days like this remind me why I love working with this team at Tidewater.

Six months ago we promised customers that alerts would arrive with a reason attached, not just a red number. Last night we turned that on for everyone. ✨

Every alert now says what changed, which service it touched first and which past incident it most resembles. Our own on-call engineers have been testing it since August, and the feedback that stuck with me came from Dev Ranganathan: “I went back to sleep because I could see it was the same disk problem as June.” That is exactly the outcome we were aiming for — fewer people woken up for things that can wait until morning.

A few numbers from the trial:
Pages per engineer per week fell from eleven to four.
Median time to the first useful note on an incident dropped from 19 minutes to 6.
Not one of the alerts we suppressed turned out to matter. 

Huge thanks to the people who made it happen: Ingrid, who argued for plain language in every message; Kofi, who rebuilt the event pipeline so the context arrives within seconds; and the twelve customer teams who let us watch their worst nights.

We also picked up the Southern Lights award for operations tooling along the way, which was a lovely surprise. 🏆

There’s plenty still to do. Next up is letting teams teach the system which changes they consider risky, and showing the reasoning behind every grouping.

If you run on-call for a living, try it and tell us where it’s wrong. 💚

Onward to the next release 🚀

text:
🚀 𝗦𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝘂𝘇𝘇𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝘄𝗼 𝗯𝗶𝗴 𝗱𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗞𝗶𝘄𝗶 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗔𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗲 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗪𝗲𝗲𝗸 🇦🇺🇳🇿

More than 600 founders, engineers and researchers came together in Wellington to compare notes on building software that lasts. I’ve been to plenty of conferences, but few where the hallway conversations were this honest about what went wrong.

𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗜 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗵𝗼𝗺𝗲: 
𝟭. 𝗦𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗺𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝗻 𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀. The best demos came from groups of three or four who picked one problem and refused to drift.
𝟮. 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘄 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴. Almost every talk on AI products spent more time on how they measure quality than on the model itself.
𝟯. 𝗥𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁. Selling to a hospital in Dunedin is not the same as selling to one in Dallas, and the teams that accept that early grow faster. 

A special thank you to the organisers, who ran the whole thing with volunteers and still managed to keep every session on time. 💥

If you missed it, the talk recordings go up next week, and I’ll share my full notes in a longer write-up. 

Already counting down to next year.

#BuildersWeek #StartupLife #NewZealand #Australia #AIEngineering #Founders #ProductDevelopment #Community #TechEvents

As part of that, we’re opening an office in Brisbane early next year and doubling the number of engineers in Melbourne. Customers here asked for local support, local data storage and someone they can call in their own time zone, and that is what we are building.

What is new this quarter:
Data residency in Sydney and Melbourne regions: https://bramblecone.example.com/residency
A local partner programme for consultancies: https://bramblecone.example.com/partners
Free evaluation workshops for public sector teams: https://bramblecone.example.com/workshops 
Our first Australian customer advisory board: https://bramblecone.example.com/advisory

We also published the results of our independent security assessment, including the findings we have not finished fixing yet: https://bramblecone.example.com/assessment-2026

If you’d like to join us, the open roles are listed here: https://bramblecone.example.com/careers 
And if you are a customer with questions about the move, my calendar is open: https://bramblecone.example.com/meet

Thank you to everyone who has trusted a small team from the other side of the world. We intend to earn it.

text:
Some personal news 🎊

After eight years in consulting, I’ve started my own security testing practice: Kestrel Ridge Assurance.

The plan is simple. Small and medium businesses get the same careful testing that large companies pay for, at a price they can plan around.

What I offer:
🔸 Web application testing 
🔸 Cloud configuration reviews
🔸 Phishing exercises with follow-up training 
🔸 Plain-language reports your board can read

A standard web assessment is a fixed $4,500, with a free retest once you have fixed the findings.

Every engagement starts with a short call about what you actually need protected, and ends with a session where I walk your team through each finding and how to fix it. No jargon, no fear tactics, and no report that sits unread in a shared drive.

Thank you to the mentors who told me to stop waiting for the perfect moment, and to the first three clients who signed up before I had a logo.

If you know a business that has never had a proper security test, I’d be grateful for an introduction. 

Here’s to the next chapter.

#CyberSecurity #PenetrationTesting #SmallBusiness #NewBeginnings #InfoSec #Australia
